facts.summary: Arkansas's state minimum wage is $11.00 per hour, higher than the federal $7.25.
facts.citation: Ark. Code Ann. §§ 11-4-201 et seq. (Arkansas Minimum Wage Act)
facts.sourceAgency: Arkansas Department of Labor and Licensing, Labor Standards Division
facts.notes: $11.00 since Jan 1, 2021; Arkansas has no scheduled annual increases. Tipped cash wage is $2.63/hr (tips must reach the applicable minimum). Verify no 2026 legislative change.

facts.summary: The Arkansas Minimum Wage Act applies to employers with four or more employees (lower than nothing in FLSA, which uses commerce tests).
facts.sourceAgency: Arkansas Department of Labor and Licensing, Labor Standards Division
facts.notes: Employers with fewer than 4 employees fall outside the state Act; FLSA may still apply. The higher of state or federal minimum wage governs for each employee.

facts.summary: Arkansas has no daily overtime; overtime is 1.5x pay after 40 hours in a workweek and white-collar exemptions track the federal FLSA salary level.
facts.citation: Ark. Code Ann. §§ 11-4-201 et seq.; AR DOL Minimum Wage & Overtime Rules
facts.sourceAgency: Arkansas Department of Labor and Licensing, Labor Standards Division
facts.notes: No daily OT rule. Weekly threshold is 40 hours actually worked (paid leave does not count). Executive/administrative/professional/outside-sales exemptions mirror the FLSA, including the $684/week salary level. Applies to employers with 4+ employees.

facts.summary: The Arkansas Civil Rights Act prohibits employment discrimination based on race, religion, national origin/ancestry, gender, and disability.
facts.citation: Ark. Code Ann. § 16-123-107 (Arkansas Civil Rights Act of 1993)
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Commission on Civil Rights (review of the Arkansas Civil Rights Act)
facts.notes: Gender is generally read to include pregnancy. ACRA does NOT cover age (age claims proceed under federal ADEA), sexual orientation, or gender identity. Source is a 2001 federal review; confirm current classes against the live statute text of § 16-123-107.

facts.summary: The Arkansas Civil Rights Act covers employers with 9 or more employees in Arkansas in each of 20 or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year -- a lower threshold than federal Title VII/ADA's 15-employee floor, though still higher than a 1-employee floor.
facts.citation: Ark. Code Ann. § 16-123-102(5) (as enacted, Act 962 of 1993, § 3)
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary enacting-Act PDF (Act 962 of 1993, Section 3, definition of 'Employer'): 'a person who employs nine (9) or more employees in the State of Arkansas in each of twenty (20) or more calendar weeks in the current or preceding calendar year.' The current codified subsection letter/number (secondary sources cite it as both (5) and (7) depending on year) was not independently re-verified against a live, freely-accessible official Arkansas Code portal this session -- no such reliably fetchable free official full-text code site was found (see also final-pay and deadlines.wageClaim notes in this file). VERIFY the current subsection citation if precision on the subsection letter matters.

facts.value: no state administrative agency (court filing only)
facts.summary: Arkansas has no state fair-employment agency; ACRA claims are filed directly in court (no state administrative charge deadline), while federal charges go to the EEOC.
facts.citation: Ark. Code Ann. § 16-123-107(c) (Arkansas Civil Rights Act of 1993)
facts.sourceAgency: U.S. Commission on Civil Rights (review of the Arkansas Civil Rights Act)
facts.notes: There is no Arkansas FEPA; the ACRA is enforced through private lawsuits. Reported (aggregator) rule under § 16-123-107(c): an ACRA employment action must be brought within 1 year of the discrimination or within 90 days of an EEOC right-to-sue letter, whichever is later — verify against live statute. Federal EEOC charge deadline remains 180/300 days.

facts.summary: The Arkansas Whistle-Blower Act protects public employees from retaliation for good-faith reporting of waste or violations of law; there is no general private-sector whistleblower statute.
facts.citation: Ark. Code Ann. §§ 21-1-601 to -610 (Arkansas Whistle-Blower Act)
facts.sourceAgency: Arkansas Department of Transformation and Shared Services
facts.notes: Covers public employers/employees only. Private-sector employees rely on federal statutes or the common-law public-policy exception to at-will employment. Official PDF could not be auto-parsed; citation corroborated by multiple Arkansas state sources — verify statute text.

facts.value: next regular payday; 7 days if employee demands payment
facts.summary: When an employee is discharged, Arkansas requires payment of wages due by the next regular payday; if the employee requests payment and the employer fails to pay within 7 days of that payday, the employer owes double the unpaid wages as a penalty.
facts.sourceAgency: Arkansas Department of Labor and Licensing, Labor Standards Division
facts.notes: Statute text confirmed via multiple consistent secondary legal summaries (Ark. Code Ann. 11-4-405); the section applies expressly to discharge, and Arkansas case law/DOL guidance treats voluntary resignation the same way absent a separate statute -- verify directly against primary Arkansas Code text if possible (no reliably fetchable official full-text statute portal was found this session; law.arkansas.gov and ago.arkansas.gov did not resolve for this tool).

facts.value: DOL investigates claims of $2,000 or less; private suits must be filed within ~3 years
facts.summary: The Labor Standards Division administratively investigates wage claims of $2,000 or less (often final-paycheck disputes); private minimum-wage suits carry a judicially established 3-year limitations period.
facts.citation: Ark. Code Ann. §§ 11-4-201 et seq.; Douglas v. First Student, Inc. (Ark. 2011)
facts.sourceAgency: Arkansas Department of Labor and Licensing, Labor Standards Division
facts.notes: DOL administrative wage claims are capped at $2,000 (confirmed on the DOL page). The 3-year statute of limitations for private Arkansas Minimum Wage Act suits is court-established (Douglas v. First Student) and not stated on an official code page — verify.
